841.title: The king who saw heaven and hell
841.hook: King Nemi is shown both, and returns to govern well (Jataka 541)
841.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching describes heavens and hells as places beings pass through according to their deeds, not as final destinations; the Nimi story is told to show how actions shape what follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sama, shot at the river, thought first of his blind parents. Your line was who will bring them water. Did you do the small thing for the one who raised you? Today, a new week, and a king given a ride through other worlds. Day eight hundred forty-one.

A chariot comes down out of the sky for a king. That's how this tale turns. King Nimi of Mithila gives freely and keeps the precepts, and the story says even the gods start talking about him. Sakka, their king, wants to meet him, so he sends his own charioteer, Matali, to bring Nimi up. On the way, Matali asks a question: which road would you like to take? Today, the road Nimi chose, and why he came home.
screen: `A CHARIOT FROM THE SKY.` → `THE GODS TALK OF NIMI.` → `WHICH ROAD FIRST?`

segments.voice: First, the hells. Nimi asks to see both roads, and Matali drives him past the hells first, and at each one Nimi asks the same question: what did these beings do? Matali answers, deed by deed. Cruelty, cheating, harm done to the weak. The tale doesn't linger for horror's sake. It's a map of where actions lead. Second, the heavens. Then the chariot rises, and Nimi sees mansions of light. Again he asks, what did these beings do? And again the answer is deeds: gifts given, precepts kept, kindness shown. Third, the offer. In Sakka's heaven, Nimi is welcomed and invited to stay. And he says no. A reward he hasn't earned, he says, would be like something borrowed; he'd rather go home and do the good himself. Fourth, the return. So Matali brings him back to Mithila, and Nimi tells his people what he saw, and goes on ruling, and giving, and keeping his vows. Tradition pairs this tale with the perfection of resolve, adhitthana: a decision that holds. Given a glimpse of how things end, a person might want to skip straight to the good part. Nimi uses the glimpse to go back to work. He knows where the road leads, so he walks it on purpose, and the ordinary days of ruling are where it happens.
screen: `THE HELLS: WHAT DID THEY DO?` · `THE HEAVENS: WHAT DID THEY DO?` · `NO TO A BORROWED REWARD.` · `HOME TO MITHILA, TO WORK.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK TO RULE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at today from its end. Let the breath settle. Picture tonight, just before sleep, looking back over this day. What would you be glad it held? A finished task, a kind word, patience in one hard moment. Let one answer come clearly. Then come back to now, to this ordinary hour, and notice that this is where that end gets made. No skipping ahead. Just the next step, taken knowing where it leads. The bell holds the time.
Adhitthana. Resolve: the perfection King Nimi showed, shown where deeds lead, who turned down a reward and went home to do good himself. Today's word.
Your line: he came back to rule. Do the one thing you'd be glad tonight's look-back would find, while it's still an ordinary hour. Day eight hundred forty-one.

screen: `DAY 841 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PRINCE SET FOR SACRIFICE.`

fork.reveal: he declines; a reward he didn't earn would be like something borrowed, so he goes back to Mithila and rules well.

original.note: Pali adhitthana, resolve: the perfection tradition pairs with Nimi's tale.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tour of heaven and hell meant to scare people straight.
what it means: a king shown where deeds lead, who turns down a free reward and goes home to do good himself.
what a scholar hears: in Jataka 541 every world is explained by deeds, so heavens and hells are results, not prizes; tradition pairs the tale with resolve, adhitthana.

842.title: The prince set for sacrifice
842.hook: Candakumara, marked for a sacrifice by a wicked priest, saved by truth (Jataka 542)
842.tomorrow: The serpent who kept the precepts
842.howItsDone: The tale of Canda (also called the Khandahala Jataka) is told as an example of the perfection of patience; Buddhist ethics begins with the precept of not harming living beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Nimi's adhitthana, his resolve, saw where deeds lead and went home to do the work. Your line was he came back to rule. Did you do the thing tonight's look-back would want? Today, a prince who stands where cruelty is about to happen. Day eight hundred forty-two.

A courtroom, and a judge who sells his verdicts. He is Khandahala, the king's chaplain, and he takes bribes; whoever pays wins. One day a man who has been cheated walks out weeping and meets Prince Canda, who hears the case again and gives the true verdict. The crowd cheers the prince for an honest judgment. Khandahala says nothing at all, and waits for his chance. Today, what a resentful man does with a king's fear, and what stops him.
screen: `A JUDGE WHO TAKES BRIBES.` → `THE PRINCE HEARS IT AGAIN.` → `KHANDAHALA WAITS.`

segments.voice: First, the grudge finds its chance. The king dreams of heaven and asks Khandahala the way there. The chaplain sees his opening. A great sacrifice, he says: the king's own children, queens, wealthy citizens, and animals, Prince Canda among them. Second, the pleading. Canda doesn't rage. He begs his father, reasons with him, reminds him of everything between them. The people weep in the streets. The story lets the king waver, ordering the prisoners freed, then taken back again, as Khandahala works on his fear. Third, the act of truth. At the place of sacrifice, with the blade raised, Canda's wife speaks. She declares the truth of her life and asks that, by that truth, the harm be stopped. And Sakka, king of the gods, comes blazing down and terrifies the king into letting them go. Fourth, the ending. The crowd turns on the chaplain, the king is driven out, and Canda is made king. Tradition pairs this tale with patience, khanti. Canda's patience isn't silence. He speaks the whole time, clearly, without hatred, to the man about to kill him. The story is about cruelty dressed up as a sacred duty, and it puts its hope in two things: a person who keeps pleading without hating, and words that are true.
screen: `A DREAM, AND A CRUEL ANSWER.` · `CANDA PLEADS WITHOUT HATE.` · `HIS WIFE SPEAKS THE TRUTH.` · `THE CRUELTY IS STOPPED.` · then, large: `SAVED BY TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one cruelty you could name. Breathe out slowly once or twice. Think of a small unkindness near you that's gone unchallenged. A joke at someone's expense. A rule that hurts someone quietly. A way people talk about a coworker. Don't reach for the biggest injustice in the world. Choose one close enough to touch. Then picture saying something true about it, calmly, without contempt for anyone, the way Canda pleaded. Just one sentence. Rehearse it in your mind until it sounds like you. The bell holds the time.
Khanti. Patience: what Canda, marked to die for a chaplain's grudge, kept as he pleaded without hatred, before his wife's act of truth saved him. Today's word.
Your line: saved by truth. If the moment comes today, say your one calm, true sentence about the cruelty you named. Day eight hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 842 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SERPENT WHO KEPT THE PRECEPTS.`

original.note: Pali khanti, patience: the perfection tradition pairs with Canda's tale.

what it means: cruelty dressed up as sacred duty, met by patient pleading and stopped by words that are true.
what a scholar hears: in Jataka 542 patience means speaking without hatred, not staying silent; tradition counts the tale among the last ten great Jatakas, each paired with a perfection.

sources.ref: Jataka 542 (Khandahala Jataka, the tale of Candakumara)

843.title: The serpent who kept the precepts
843.hook: the naga prince Bhuridatta keeps the uposatha even when captured (Jataka 543)
843.howItsDone: On uposatha days, tied to the phases of the moon, Buddhist lay people may visit a temple, listen to teaching, and take extra precepts for the day and night, such as eating no food after midday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Prince Canda's khanti, his patience, held as his wife's true words stopped a sacrifice. Your line was saved by truth. Did you find your one calm sentence? Today, someone who keeps a vow with his life on the line. Day eight hundred forty-three.

A great snake lies coiled on top of an anthill by a river, perfectly still. He isn't hunting, and he isn't asleep. He's keeping a holy day. In the Jataka he is Bhuridatta, a prince of the nagas, the serpent beings of the waters, and he has come up into the human world to keep the observance without distraction. He has made a vow about anyone who finds him there. Today, someone does.
screen: `A SNAKE ON AN ANTHILL.` → `KEEPING A HOLY DAY.` → `A VOW ABOUT ANYONE WHO COMES.`

segments.voice: First, the observance. The uposatha is the Buddhist observance day, when lay people take on extra precepts and keep them for the day and night. Bhuridatta keeps it seriously. His vow, the story says, is that if anyone wants his skin, his flesh, anything at all, they can take it; he won't break his precepts to stop them. Second, the betrayal. A hunter who knows where he lies betrays him to a snake charmer, in a bargain over a magic jewel. The charmer seizes him and crushes him into a basket. Third, the test. Bhuridatta has the power to destroy his captor, the story says, with a single angry look. He won't give him even that. He keeps his eyes shut rather than look at the man in anger, so his precept holds. The charmer drags him from village to village and makes him dance for coins, and still he keeps it. Fourth, the rescue. His family searches for him, finds him, and wins him free. Tradition pairs this tale with sila, virtue. Notice what kind of virtue it is. Not a show of goodness for an audience, but a line kept when breaking it would be easy and would even seem fair. The precept isn't tested on a quiet day. It's tested in the basket.
screen: `THE OBSERVANCE DAY AND HIS VOW.` · `BETRAYED TO A SNAKE CHARMER.` · `NOT EVEN AN ANGRY LOOK.` · `HIS FAMILY WINS HIM FREE.` · then, large: `HE KEPT IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one line to keep today. Let the breath settle. Pick a single precept, something like not speaking falsely, not taking what isn't given, or a promise you keep with yourself. Now picture the moment today when it'll be hardest: the meeting, the conversation, the shortcut that's right there. See yourself in that moment, keeping it, quietly, the way the serpent kept his eyes closed. No speech, no drama. Just the line, held. The bell holds the time.
Uposatha. The observance day Bhuridatta the naga prince was keeping when, captured and mistreated, he wouldn't even look at his captor in anger. Today's word.
Your line: he kept it. When the hard moment you pictured arrives, keep your one line, and let no one need to know. Day eight hundred forty-three.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy tale about a magic snake.
what it means: a vow kept when breaking it would be easy and even seem fair; virtue tested in the basket, not on a quiet day.
what a scholar hears: tradition pairs Jataka 543 with sila, virtue, and its hero is a naga keeping the lay observance day.

844.title: The daughter who argued
844.hook: Princess Ruja rescues her father from a false teaching (Jataka 544)
844.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching holds that intentional actions, kamma, bear fruit; the tale of Ruja and Narada is told to show why that teaching matters for how a person lives and gives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a naga prince kept his uposatha in a snake charmer's basket. Your line was he kept it. Did your one line hold when it got hard? Today, a princess who won't let her father's mistake stand. Day eight hundred forty-four.

On a bright festival night, King Angati of Mithila asks his advisers what would make the evening complete. One suggests visiting a famous ascetic. The king goes, and the ascetic, Guna, tells him something that sounds like freedom: there is no fruit of deeds. Good or bad, nothing you do comes back. What will be, will be. The king goes home convinced. Today, the person who argues him out of it: his daughter.
screen: `A FESTIVAL NIGHT.` → `NO FRUIT OF DEEDS.` → `THE KING IS CONVINCED.`

segments.voice: First, what the teaching does. Angati stops giving. He closes his gifts to the poor and turns to his own pleasures, since nothing, he now believes, makes a difference. Second, the daughter. Princess Ruja comes to him, as she regularly does, to ask for money for her own gifts. He refuses and explains his new view. And she argues. Respectfully, calling him father, but she doesn't back down. The story says she could remember past lives, and she tells him of one where a wrong she did came back to her in suffering. Deeds have fruit, she says; she has seen it. Third, she can't win alone. The king won't move. So Ruja doesn't give up; she turns to the directions and asks, in effect, for any good being in the world to come and help. Fourth, the help. Narada, a being from a high heaven, comes down dressed as an ascetic, and with patience and vivid pictures of where deeds lead, brings the king back to giving and to his precepts. Tradition pairs this tale with equanimity, upekkha. The one who stands up to the false teaching in the palace isn't a sage or a minister. It's a daughter, speaking up at home, to her own father, with no guarantee he'll listen. She argues with love, not contempt, and she asks for help when her own words run out. That's the shape of disagreeing well.
screen: `THE KING STOPS GIVING.` · `RUJA ARGUES, RESPECTFULLY.` · `SHE ASKS FOR HELP.` · `NARADA BRINGS HIM BACK.` · then, large: `THE DAUGHTER ARGUED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one belief gently. Sit upright and let the shoulders drop. Choose a belief of your own, something small you've taken as settled. Nothing changes anyway. They'll never listen. I'm just not that kind of person. Hold it up to the light. Is it true? What have you actually seen? Don't attack it, and don't defend it. Just ask, the way Ruja asked her father, with respect and without backing down. Let whatever answer comes sit there, unhurried. The bell holds the time.
The daughter who argued. Princess Ruja, who stood up to her father's false teaching with respect and asked for help when her words ran out. Today's word.
Your line: the daughter argued. Before tonight, check the belief you questioned against one thing that actually happens today. Day eight hundred forty-four.

what it means: a daughter refuses a false teaching at home, with respect, and asks for help when her own words run out.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 544, tradition's tale of equanimity, upekkha, sets a teaching that denies the fruit of deeds against the Buddhist teaching of kamma.

845.title: The wise minister
845.hook: Vidhura is won at dice by a spirit and teaches him on the way (Jataka 545)
845.howItsDone: Vidhura's story is told as an example of the perfection of truth; in Buddhist practice, sharing the teaching is valued as a gift in itself, the gift of the Dhamma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Princess Ruja stood up to her father's false teaching. Your line was the daughter argued. Did the belief you questioned hold up against the day? Today, a wise man lost in a game of dice. Day eight hundred forty-five.

A stranger arrives at the king's court with a jewel and a horse that can run through the sky, and offers a game of dice. If he loses, the king takes both. If he wins, he wants one thing: the king's minister, Vidhura, known across the kingdom for his wisdom. The king rolls, and loses. The stranger is a yakkha, a fierce spirit, named Punnaka. Today, where he takes Vidhura, and what happens on the way.
screen: `A JEWEL, A SKY-HORSE, DICE.` → `THE STAKE: VIDHURA.` → `THE KING LOSES.`

segments.voice: First, the wish behind it all. Far below, in the realm of the nagas, a queen named Vimala has heard Vidhura speak about goodness, and she longs for his heart. Her daughter, Irandati, offers to marry whoever brings it, and Punnaka sets out to get it. Second, the misunderstanding. Punnaka takes the word literally. On the journey, with Vidhura clinging to the horse's tail through the sky, he tries to frighten the minister to death, and finally tries to dash him from a mountaintop. Vidhura stays unshaken, and asks a calm question: why are you doing this? Third, the teaching. Punnaka tells him. And instead of pleading for his life, Vidhura teaches him: how a good person lives, keeps faith with friends, and repays kindness. Punnaka is changed. He offers to take Vidhura home. Vidhura says no; take me to the nagas, as you promised. Fourth, the heart. In the naga palace it comes out at last. The queen never wanted flesh. The heart she longed for was his wisdom, and Vidhura gives it, teaching the naga king and queen, and then goes home. Tradition pairs this tale with truth, sacca. What's striking is where the teaching happens. Not in a temple, not at court. In the hands of someone trying to kill him, on a mountaintop, in the middle of the worst day of his life. Vidhura treats even that as a place to teach.
screen: `A QUEEN LONGS FOR HIS HEART.` · `DANGLED FROM A MOUNTAINTOP.` · `HE TEACHES HIS WOULD-BE KILLER.` · `THE HEART WAS HIS WISDOM.` · then, large: `HE TAUGHT HIS CAPTOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the place you're being taken. Let the breath settle. Think of somewhere today will put you that you didn't choose. A meeting, a long commute, a waiting room, a hard conversation. Picture yourself there. Now ask: what could I offer here? Not a lecture. Patience, a steady voice, one useful thing you know, a question asked kindly. Let one answer settle. Rest with the picture of being useful exactly where you didn't want to be. The bell holds the time.
Pandita. A wise one: what Vidhura was called, won at dice and carried off by a spirit who meant to kill him, and taught his captor instead. Today's word.
Your line: he taught his captor. In the place you didn't choose today, offer the one useful thing you pictured. Day eight hundred forty-five.

846.title: The clever sage
846.hook: Mahosadha solves the court's riddles and saves the kingdom by wit (Jataka 546)
846.howItsDone: The Mahosadha story is told as a tale of practical wisdom; in Buddhist teaching, wisdom (panna) is one of the ten perfections.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vidhura, the pandita, was won at dice and taught the spirit who carried him off. Your line was he taught his captor. Did you offer something useful where you didn't choose to be? Today, a boy who solves things. Day eight hundred forty-six.

Two women, one baby, and a judge who is still a child. Each woman swears the baby is hers. Nobody saw what happened. In the Jataka the judge is a village boy named Mahosadha, who has built a hall where people bring their quarrels, and this is one of them. He doesn't ask for witnesses. He draws a line on the ground. Today, what the line is for, and how a boy's wit ends up saving a kingdom.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE BABY.` → `A BOY JUDGE.` → `A LINE ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the name. The story says he was born holding a healing herb, and so he was called Mahosadha, great medicine. It's a fitting name for someone whose gift is fixing things. Second, the cases. Back to the line. He places the baby on it and tells the women to pull, one by the arms, one by the legs; whoever pulls the child across keeps him. They pull. The baby cries out. And one woman lets go, rather than hurt him. That, the boy says, is the mother. The other, the story reveals, wasn't human at all. Case after case goes like that: he finds the answer by watching how people act, not by guessing. Third, the court. Word reaches King Vedeha of Mithila, who brings the boy to court. There, jealous advisers test him, scheme against him, try to get him thrown out. He keeps answering riddles, keeps seeing through traps. Fourth, the kingdom. When a rival king threatens Mithila, Mahosadha's plan, a great tunnel, the ummagga the tale is named for, turns a trap into a peace and saves his king. Tradition pairs this tale with wisdom, panna. What's notable is the kind of wisdom. It's practical. It reads people. And it's always used to protect someone: the baby, the cheated, the king. The baby goes home with the woman who let go.
screen: `BORN HOLDING A HEALING HERB.` · `THE MOTHER LETS GO.` · `RIDDLES AND TRAPS AT COURT.` · `A GREAT TUNNEL SAVES THE KING.` · then, large: `WIT THAT SAVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch, don't guess. Rest your hands and let the room go quiet. Bring to mind one person whose mood or need you've been guessing at lately. A child, a coworker, a friend who's gone quiet. Set the guesses aside. Recall only what they actually did this week: what they reached for, what they avoided, when they lit up. Let their actions tell you something, the way the mother's letting go told Mahosadha. Find one small, practical way to help that fits what you saw. The bell holds the time.
Panna. Wisdom: what Mahosadha the boy judge showed, reading people well and using his wit to protect them, all the way to saving his king. Today's word.
Your line: wit that saves. Try the one small help you found, and watch what the person does, not just what they say. Day eight hundred forty-six.

847.title: Vessantara, read whole
847.hook: the generous prince's tale, read from the white elephant to the homecoming (Jataka 547)
847.howItsDone: In Theravada lands the Vessantara tale is retold, chanted and painted, and some communities recite it in full at a yearly festival as a teaching on generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the clever sage, panna itself. Your line was wit that saves. This week brought a king shown heaven and hell, a prince saved by truth, a serpent who kept his vows, a daughter who argued, a minister who taught his captor, and that clever sage. Today, the tale they lead to. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

The elephant is white, and the people of the Sivi kingdom say it brings the rain. One morning, envoys arrive from Kalinga, a land dried out by drought, and they ask the crown prince for it. The prince pours water over their hands to seal the gift and hands the elephant over. By evening the city is furious, and the king is pressed to send his own son into exile. The prince is Vessantara. Tradition places his tale at the end of the Jataka and tells it as the bodhisatta's last life before the one in which he became the Buddha. Today we read it whole.
screen: `A WHITE ELEPHANT, GIVEN AWAY.` → `A CITY IN UPROAR.` → `A PRINCE SENT INTO EXILE.`

segments.voice: First, the road out. Vessantara leaves with his wife Maddi and their two small children, Jali and Kanhajina. He gives away his wealth before he goes, and on the road he gives away the chariot and the horses too, so the family walks. They settle in huts on a mountain called Vankagiri and live simply. Second, the hardest gift. An old brahmin named Jujaka, pushed by a young wife who wants servants, finds the hermitage while Maddi is out gathering fruit, and he asks for the children. Vessantara gives them. What Maddi finds when she comes home belongs to tomorrow, so we leave that scene for now. Third, the last test. The god Sakka arrives disguised as a brahmin and asks for Maddi herself. Vessantara gives her too, and Sakka at once gives her back and shows who he is. Fourth, the homecoming. Jujaka leads the children to their grandfather, the king, who ransoms them. The whole court goes up the mountain, the family is together again, and Vessantara returns as king. In the telling, the earth shakes at his gifts. This is a hard tale, and Buddhists have said so themselves. In the Questions of King Milinda, a king asks the monk Nagasena about it directly: was giving away the children not cruel? Nagasena answers by calling it a gift almost too great to do, made for the sake of awakening. Some readers hear in it dana, generosity, carried to its very edge. Others point out that the tale itself never hides the cost: the children's fear and the mother's grief are told in full. Read in pieces, it can sound like a parable about letting go. Read whole, it holds the gift and what the gift costs, and it ends with everyone home.

Tell it out loud in your own words, slowly, in a few sentences, as if to a child at bedtime. Notice which scene you chose, and which ones you passed over.
